question: What is another widely used name for disseminated sclerosis?
explanation: Disseminated sclerosis is the older or alternative term for multiple sclerosis, a condition marked by widespread nervous system damage. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why do symptoms of disseminated sclerosis differ so much from one patient to another?

options.A: Damage occurs randomly across different areas of the central nervous system
options.B: Different patients have completely different blood types
options.C: The disease only affects the peripheral nerves in the arms and legs
options.D: Infection rates change depending on the weather

explanation: Think of it like scars forming in different places in the brain or spinal cord. The symptoms depend entirely on which exact nerve pathways are affected! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h1)

question: Which part of the nerve cell is mainly destroyed during the demyelination process in disseminated sclerosis?
explanation: You've got this! The immune system mistakenly attacks and strips away the myelin sheath, which normally acts like an insulation cover to protect nerves and speed up signals. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h2)

question: How do hard scars (plaques) cause symptoms in disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: They cause excess production of spinal fluid in the brain ventricles
options.B: They stimulate muscles to contract constantly without rest
options.C: They repair the damaged nerves completely back to normal
options.D: They block and slow down electrical signals traveling along nerve fibers

explanation: When inflammation creates scar tissue (plaques), it gets in the way of smooth electrical conduction—leading to the physical and sensory changes patients feel. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h2)

question: Which group of people is diagnosed with disseminated sclerosis more often?
explanation: Studies consistently show that disseminated sclerosis affects women about twice as often as men. Good to keep in mind for your exams! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which of the following is linked as an environmental trigger for developing MS?

options.A: Living close to sea level in tropical zones
options.B: Engaging in heavy physical labor outdoors
options.C: Eating a diet high in processed carbohydrates
options.D: Past viral infections like Epstein-Barr virus

explanation: While the exact cause isn't fully pinned down, certain past viral infections are believed to help trigger this abnormal immune response in vulnerable people. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is a very common early sign that patients with developing disseminated sclerosis report?
explanation: Keep an eye out for this: inflammation of the optic nerve causing blurry vision or eye pain is frequently one of the very first warning signs of MS. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h4)

question: A patient has sudden flare-ups of numbness and weakness that completely clear up after a few weeks, followed by long periods of normal health. What pattern is this?
explanation: This is the classic 'relapsing-remitting' pattern—clear flare-ups (relapses) followed by periods where the patient recovers and feels fine (remissions). [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h4)

question: What is the main imaging test doctors use to see brain and spinal cord plaques in disseminated sclerosis?
explanation: An MRI is the gold standard here because it gives a clear picture of scarring and inflammation inside the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h5)

question: Why would a doctor perform a lumbar puncture (spinal tap) when investigating suspected disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: To drain excess blood following an acute head injury
options.B: To check cerebrospinal fluid for signs of abnormal immune activity
options.C: To inject medication that stops nerve pain immediately
options.D: To measure the exact pressure inside the heart chambers

explanation: Testing the spinal fluid helps find specific markers (like oligoclonal bands) that point straight to inflammation in the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h5)

question: Which medication class is quickly given to calm down inflammation during a sudden MS flare-up?
explanation: High-dose corticosteroids are the go-to treatment to quickly quiet down acute inflammation when a patient has a relapse. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is the main goal of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) in treating disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: To immediately repair severed nerve axons overnight
options.B: To reduce relapse frequency and slow long-term disability
options.C: To completely cure the underlying autoimmune response
options.D: To lower elevated blood pressure caused by stress

explanation: While they don't offer an instant cure, DMTs help calm the immune system over time, preventing future attacks and keeping the patient independent longer. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is a key nursing care action for a patient dealing with extreme fatigue from disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: Keeping the patient confined strictly to bed
options.B: Restricting all fluid intake after midday
options.C: Scheduling planned rest periods throughout the day

explanation: Pacing is everything! Balancing daily activities with scheduled rest helps patients conserve their energy without burning out. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h7)

question: For a patient with severe mobility problems due to disseminated sclerosis, which complication should nurses watch out for and prevent?
explanation: When patients spend a lot of time in bed or a wheelchair, their skin is at high risk. Regular turning and meticulous skin care are vital nursing duties! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of physiotherapy in long-term MS care?

options.A: Maintaining mobility and preventing joint stiffness
options.C: Performing surgical repair of demyelinated nerves

explanation: Physiotherapy keeps muscles working, improves balance, and prevents tight joints (contractures), helping the patient stay active for as long as possible. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h8)

question: Why is a multidisciplinary team (doctors, nurses, physiotherapists) so important for patients with advanced disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: Physicians are not permitted to manage neurological disorders alone
options.B: The disease affects many different physical, cognitive, and emotional functions
options.C: It eliminates the need for any ongoing medical drug therapy
options.D: Patients require daily surgical procedures to replace damaged nerves

explanation: Because MS touches movement, speech, mood, and daily living, it takes a whole team of specialists working together to give the patient the best quality of life. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h8)
